item.title: Self-Hosted WebAssembly Runtime for Runtime-Neutral Checkpoint/Restore in Edge-Cloud Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2611.27225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Checkpoint/restore (C/R) in the Edge-Cloud Continuum, where edge servers and cloud servers are integrated to combine their respective computational characteristics, enables application live migration for load balancing and service continuity that adapts to user mobility. WebAssembly (Wasm) provides architecture neutrality, allowing bytecode execution across diverse platforms. Furthermore, by leveraging runtime implementations specialized for particular environments and performance optimizations such as JIT and AOT, Wasm bytecode can be executed efficiently by using the runtime best suited to each environment. However, the diversity of runtimes and performance optimizations results in heterogeneous representations of application execution states, making it difficult to apply C/R across multiple runtimes. To address this heterogeneity, we propose a C/R method that employs a self-hosted Wasm runtime compiled into Wasm itself. By checkpointing and restoring application execution states within the self-hosted Wasm runtime, the representation of execution states can be unified. In addition, to mitigate the overhead of duplicated runtime executions, we also investigate optimization techniques for Wasm runtimes designed to be self-hosted. Our evaluation results demonstrate that C/R with a self-hosted Wasm runtime can eliminate runtime differences and enable efficient live migration with a minimal execution state.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Nakata, Katsuya Matsubara

item.title: Bring Cloud-Native Networking to FreeBSD Jails: Porting Calico from Linux
item.description: arXiv:2611.27320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Linux containers benefit from a rich ecosystem of Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins such as Calico and Cilium, FreeBSD Jails lacked native, standardized solutions for advanced networking. As a result, users have relied on manual, error-prone configurations, limiting scalability and integration with modern orchestration platforms. This paper introduces porting Calico, a widely adopted CNI plugin, to the FreeBSD operating system. Our approach replaced Linux-specific components with FreeBSD-native equivalents: iptables with ipfw, netlink sockets with routing sockets, and Linux network namespaces with FreeBSD's vnet. This work aims to bridge the gap between Linux and BSD container networking. By providing scalable, policy-driven capabilities that are compatible with existing Linux-centric infrastructure, FreeBSD can participate more fully in the broader container networking ecosystem.
item.dc:creator: Soma Sakaguchi, Shintaro Suzuki, Yuki Nakata, Katsuya Matsubara

item.title: A code-level survey of CPU scheduling mechanisms in open-source embedded hypervisors
item.description: arXiv:2611.27827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtualization is increasingly used in embedded systems to consolidate mixed-criticality applications onto a single platform, relying on the hypervisor's CPU scheduler to share physical CPU (pCPU) time among virtual CPUs (vCPUs). This paper surveys ten CPU scheduling algorithms implemented in four open-source hypervisors for resource-constrained systems (Bao, Xen, ACRN, and Xvisor): static partitioning, ARINC653, Credit, Credit2, RTDS, Priority-based, BVT, IORR, PRR, and PRM. Analyzed at the source-code level without runtime measurements, each algorithm is characterized by its decision rule, parameters, selection criterion, triggers, and admission control. They are evaluated against nine criteria (temporal isolation, real-time guarantees, I/O responsiveness, resource utilization, fairness, mixed-criticality support, efficiency/scalability, configurability, and multicore support) and illustrated on a common single-pCPU workload. Source-code inspection reveals key deviations from documented designs: ACRN's default BVT scheduler lacks the warp mechanism, its priority-based scheduler exposes only two priority levels, and apart from ARINC653's static frame check, only Xen's development-branch RTDS performs utilization-based admission control. Furthermore, no policy natively supports criticality attributes or mode changes, requiring integrators to encode criticality via partitions, budgets, caps, or priorities. Finally, a qualitative matrix and a decision tree guide system integrators.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Mignerey, Anthony Ferrari, Damien Sauveron, Karim Tamine

item.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
item.dc:creator: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
